strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel, analytically tractable model (Bayesian linear regression with a reward-weighted, temperature-controlled sampler) for inference-time scaling, filling a real gap in the theoretical understanding of best-of-k/LLM-as-a-judge selection.

Rigorous use of high-dimensional statistics tools (deterministic equivalents, cumulant/series expansions, extreme value theory) to derive closed-form or asymptotic expressions for generalization error as a function of n, d, k, T, and reward misspecification.

Derives several concrete, falsifiable predictions: monotonic vs. non-monotonic dependence of error on k depending on reward quality, existence of a finite optimal k under misalignment, existence of an optimal sampling temperature, the fact that the optimal reward generally differs from the true teacher, and Θ(1/k^2) decay for best-of-k with the true reward.

Provides fairly extensive internal validation of the theory against simulations of the toy model across a wide range of parameters (main text figures plus appendix G sweeps over d/n, σ/γ, S), showing the asymptotic formulas track the exact numerics well.

Attempts a bridge to practice with real LLM experiments (Llama-3-8B-Instruct as generator, Mistral-7B-Instruct as judge on GSM8K), showing qualitative existence of an optimal k and an optimal temperature, and a plausible relation between judge strength and optimal T/k shift.

Careful, transparent proof sketches with full derivations in the appendix, and a discussion of the domain of validity of each approximation (e.g., σ ≪ σ_c, high/low-T regimes), which is good practice for a paper making strong asymptotic claims.
Includes forward-looking, honest discussion of extensions (self-consistency, beam search) and current limitations of the simple i.i.d. sampling model.
weaknesses: The mapping from the linear teacher/judge/quadratic-reward toy model to real LLM-as-a-judge behavior is highly stylized; the paper's empirical LLM section only shows qualitative agreement (existence of optima) rather than any quantitative test of the specific functional forms (e.g., the 1/k^2 best-of-k law, the closed-form optimal-T or optimal-k formulas) derived in the theory, which somewhat overstates the abstract's claim of 'experimentally verifying these facts' in LLMs.

The real-world experiments are narrow in scope: a single task (GSM8K), a single generator model, and a single judge model (varied only by prompt strength), with no repeated trials/statistical testing for the weak-vs-strong judge comparison (Figure 8), limiting the generality of the qualitative claims.

The 'task difficulty' argument (Remark 6/appendix E, and the abstract's closing claim) is operationalized only through the noise scale σ in the toy model; the connection to intuitive notions of LLM task difficulty is asserted by analogy rather than demonstrated empirically.

Many of the sharpest results (Results 2, 3, Remarks 2–6) hold only in specific asymptotic regimes (large T, T→0 followed by k→∞, small σ, ample data d/n→0, flat prior) whose applicability to realistic finite-sample, finite-k LLM deployments is not clearly established.

The paper's notation is very dense with many overloaded/renormalized quantities (R, R̂, S, α, t, T, C_l, Cl(x), etc.), which combined with the length and heavy technical apparatus makes the exposition demanding and could hinder reproducibility/uptake by a broader ML audience.

The trade-off analysis between training and inference-time compute (Section 3.7, Remark 6) is derived and validated only in the toy linear model; no attempt is made to test this trade-off claim, even qualitatively, in the LLM experiments, despite it being highlighted as a key contribution in the abstract.

Practical actionability of the theory (e.g., how to actually pick k, T for a new judge/task) is not concretely demonstrated beyond the toy model; the discussion of classifier-guided reward shaping as a follow-up remains speculative and unexplored.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel, analytically tractable model (Bayesian linear regression with reward-weighted softmax selection) for studying inference-time scaling, filling a real gap in theoretical understanding of best-of-k/majority-voting style test-time compute.

Derives a rich set of closed-form results using deterministic equivalents and extreme value theory: monotonic vs. non-monotonic error in k depending on reward misalignment, existence of an optimal finite k, existence of an optimal sampling temperature T, non-optimality of the teacher reward for inference-time selection, and a Θ(1/k^2) best-of-k scaling law with explicit leading coefficient.

The theoretical predictions are cross-validated within the toy model across a wide range of parameters in the appendix (varying d/n, σ/γ, S, temperature), showing the phenomena are not artifacts of a narrow parameter regime.

The paper connects its theoretical predictions to real LLM experiments (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, and others) with two different judge models (weak/strong prompted causal LM and PRM), showing qualitatively consistent phenomena: existence of optimal k and T, and shifts in these optima with judge quality.

Provides an actionable, quantitative framework for the training-vs-inference compute trade-off (Remark 6), with explicit conditions delineating when inference-time scaling is preferable to more training data.
Comprehensive appendices with detailed proofs, additional numerical experiments, and even speculative extensions (self-consistency, beam search) that suggest a path for follow-up work.
weaknesses: The core model (linear teacher/student, quadratic reward, Gaussian data) is a substantial abstraction from actual LLM-as-a-judge settings; the mapping between the toy model's teacher weight/reward misalignment and real judge quality is asserted qualitatively but not rigorously justified or quantitatively calibrated.

LLM experiments provide only qualitative agreement with theory (existence of optima, direction of shifts) rather than quantitative validation of the closed-form formulas; in fact the authors note the empirical power-law exponent in Figure 12 does not match the theoretically predicted -2 exponent from Remark 5, undermining the sharpest quantitative claim (Θ(1/k^2)).

Several theoretical results hold only in restrictive regimes (small noise σ, large T expansion, k→∞ with T→0 taken in a specific order, small ||wR-wT||/||wT||), and it is unclear how representative these regimes are of practical LLM sampling budgets and reward-model quality.

LLM experiments are conducted on a single task/dataset (GSM8K) with a limited variety of models and reward setups; no error bars or statistical tests are reported for the "optimal k/T" claims beyond visual inspection, and some curves (e.g., Figure 8-11, Figure 23-24) appear noisy relative to the claimed non-monotonic trend, raising doubts about statistical significance.

The paper is dense and notation-heavy with many results/remarks presented somewhat tersely in the main text (proofs deferred to lengthy appendix), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility checks by readers without substantial background in random matrix theory/deterministic equivalents.

The correspondence between the theoretical "teacher" model and the real-world ground truth in the LLM experiments is left implicit (real experiments measure correctness/0-1 reward rather than distance to an explicit teacher vector), making the qualitative comparisons more heuristic than a direct empirical test of the theory.

Some proposed extensions (self-consistency, beam search, classifier-guided reward shaping) are only sketched without derivations or experiments, limiting the completeness of the contribution beyond the core i.i.d. sampling setting.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely solvable analytical model (Bayesian linear regression with reward-weighted softmax selection) for inference-time scaling, using deterministic equivalents and extreme value theory to obtain closed-form expressions for generalization error as a function of n, d, k, T, and reward misspecification.

The theoretical results are rich and internally consistent: high-T perturbative expansion, low-T best-of-k limit with a proven Θ(1/k^2) decay via extreme value theory, existence of finite optimal k under reward misalignment, existence of an optimal sampling temperature, and a quantified regime where inference-time compute is preferable to additional training data.

The paper attempts genuine empirical validation beyond the toy model, running experiments with several real LLMs (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-8B, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek-Math) and two qualitatively different judges (weak/strong causal prompts and a PRM) on GSM8K, and shows qualitative agreement with several theoretical predictions (existence of optimal k and T, judge-strength dependence of optimal T).

Extensive appendix material (proofs, additional parameter sweeps, discussion of extensions such as self-consistency and beam search) supports reproducibility and shows the phenomena hold over a fairly broad parameter range in the toy model.
weaknesses: The connection between the idealized linear teacher/quadratic-reward model and real LLM-as-a-judge behavior is only qualitative throughout; the paper itself acknowledges in Fig. 12 that the best-of-k scaling exponent measured with real models differs from the theoretically predicted k^{-2}, which undercuts the central quantitative claim (the power-law result) precisely in the setting meant to connect theory to practice.

All explicit closed-form derivations are restricted to isotropic covariance Σ = S^2 I and a linear teacher/reward with matched Gaussian noise; it is unclear how much of the qualitative story (optimal k, optimal T, reward misalignment effects) is robust to the much more complex, non-linear, non-Gaussian structure of real judges and generations.

Empirical validation is limited to a single benchmark (GSM8K) and to a custom, non-standard generalization-error metric (Eq. 27) rather than more standard evaluation protocols (e.g., pass@k, accuracy vs. compute), making it harder to compare against or reconcile with prior empirical scaling-law literature (Brown et al. 2024; Snell et al. 2025).

The paper's claims about task-difficulty degrading the inference-time-compute advantage (mentioned in the abstract and conclusion) are argued primarily from the theoretical model (via σ) rather than demonstrated with a controlled empirical difficulty sweep on real tasks, weakening the strength of this stated contribution.

The manuscript is extremely dense, packing many results/remarks with heavy notation into the main text (Results 1–3, Remarks 1–6) without a clear consolidated summary or intuition-first narrative, which could hinder accessibility despite the wealth of technical content; the appendix is very large and some proofs are only sketched.

The practical actionability of results such as "optimal reward differs from teacher" or closed-form optimal T formulas is questionable given they only strictly hold in narrow analytical regimes (t ≫ 1, small misalignment, isotropic covariance) that may not translate to real reward-model deployment, and the paper does not test whether the closed-form formulas for optimal k/T (Remarks 3, 4) numerically predict the LLM experiments' optima, only that qualitative trends match.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely tractable analytical model (Bayesian linear regression with reward-weighted softmax sampling) for a practically important but poorly understood phenomenon (inference-time scaling with LLM-as-a-judge), filling a real gap between empirical LLM inference-scaling papers and rigorous theory.

Rich, self-consistent body of theoretical results derived via deterministic equivalents and extreme value theory: closed-form posterior predictive statistics, high-temperature perturbative expansion (Result 2), low-temperature best-of-k asymptotics with a proven Θ(1/k^2) rate and explicit constant via EVT (Results 3, 5), and explicit conditions for optimal reward, optimal k, and optimal temperature (Remarks 2-4).

Extensive numerical verification of the theoretical formulas within the toy model across a wide range of parameters (Figs. 1-7, Appendix G.1), showing good quantitative agreement between theory and simulation.

Several non-obvious and interesting qualitative findings: the optimal reward for selection generally differs from the true teacher/ground truth, the existence of a distinct 'optimal temperature for the rewarding process' (as opposed to generation temperature, which is a different established notion in the literature), and a rigorous trade-off analysis of when scaling inference-time compute beats scaling training data.

Makes an effort to connect the toy model to real LLM behavior (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, multiple judges of varying quality) on GSM8K, observing qualitatively consistent phenomena (optimal k, optimal T, shift of optimal k/T with judge quality), which adds some external validity to the theoretical claims.

Detailed, careful proofs and honest proof-sketches with technical appendices; the paper is transparent about the approximations used (e.g., high-T expansion validity, small-noise regime) and explicitly states domains of validity for each result.

Includes an honest limitations/future-work discussion (Appendix F) sketching extensions to self-consistency and beam search, and openly notes open questions (training/inference trade-off in real LLMs).
weaknesses: The connection between the linear teacher-student toy model and real LLM-as-a-judge settings is quite loose: the real-LLM metric (Eq. 27, using binary correctness v(y,x) and PRM/causal-LM reward scores) is structurally different from the theoretical generalization error (squared distance to a linear teacher), so the 'agreement' claimed in Section 4 is qualitative/visual rather than quantitative or derived from an explicit mapping of parameters.

The real-LLM experiments are limited to a single dataset (GSM8K) and a modest set of open-source models/judges; no quantitative fit of theoretical formulas (e.g., predicted optimal k or T) against the empirical curves is provided, only qualitative pattern matching.

Central results (Results 2, 3, and derived Remarks 2-4) rely on several nested asymptotic/perturbative regimes (proportional limit d,n→∞, small noise σ≪σc, high-T expansion T≫s^2, or T→0 then k→∞) whose joint validity and practical relevance to real inference-time regimes (typically small-to-moderate k, non-Gaussian rewards) is not clearly established.

The isotropic covariance assumption (Σ=S^2 I) used for most closed-form and empirically-plotted results is a significant simplification; robustness to more realistic (e.g., power-law) spectra is not empirically explored, despite being an important factor in analogous kernel-regression scaling-law literature cited by the authors.

The paper's account of related literature is thorough, but the precise incremental contribution relative to closely related solvable models (e.g., Brown et al. 2024, Schaeffer et al. 2025b, Chen et al. 2024a) is not sharply delineated with head-to-head comparison of assumptions/predictions.

Presentation is dense with many results/remarks and heavy notation, which may hinder accessibility; some figures (e.g., Fig. 4, 12) show a reasonably wide match window but exact scaling exponents deviate from theory (Fig. 12 exponents differ from the Θ(1/k^2) prediction) without much discussion of why.
